```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
devtools::load_all(".")
```

For tutorial purposes, SCCNVis comes with example inputs. We will begin by
loading them and giving a brief summary of what is in each of them. Note that
the length of `cell.names` is equal to the number of rows in `input.matrix`
and that the length of `granges` is equal to the number of columns in the
`input.matrix`.

```{r setup}
library(SCCNVis)

#Example input matrix
input.matrix <- example.matrix
print(dim(input.matrix))

#Example cell names
cell.names <- example.cells
print(length(cell.names))
print(cell.names[1:3])

#Example GenomicRanges::GRanges obect
granges <- example.granges
print(granges)

#Create a SCCNVis object
obj <- SCCNVis::createPlotObject(input.matrix, cell.names, granges)
```


The SCCNVis object is a simple object. It contains the input matrix (accessible
as `obj@Matrix`) and the associated GenomicRanges::GRanges object (accessible as
`obj@GRanges`). All plotting functions withing SCCNVis use this object as input.

For example, a simple heatmap can be created using the following:

```{r}
heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj)
print(names(heatmap.result))
print(names(heatmap.result$PlotData))
```

As you can see, the result is a list object that contains the `Plot`, which is
a `ComplexHeatmap` object, and the `PlotData`. In this case, the `PlotData`
is a list containing the actual PlotData (a matrix for the heatmap) and a clustering
result, which relates to the row ordering in the heatmap. These values can be used
to create other version of the plot using other packages, or be saved for downstream 
analysis. 

The resulting file can be saved however you would normally export a `ComplexHeatmap`.
For convenience, it can be saved using the SCCNVis wrapper function for exporting plots.
The expected output for the heatmap is also shown below.
```{r eval=FALSE}
SCCNVis::saveCustomPlot(heatmap.result$Plot, "/path/to/heatmap.png")
```

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example 1a. Heatmap", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("1a_heatmap.png")
```

It is clear from the heatmap that this data has two primary subclones. A simple 
way to identify these subclones is by using the plot data from the heatmap.

```{r}
dend <- heatmap.result$PlotData$Clustering
clusters <- stats::cutree(dend, k = 2)
print(clusters[1:5])
```

One difference between these subclones was chrX. We could create a line plot
to further observe the differences between these groups on that chromosome.
I have added a few optional parameters, for additional customization. Note
that the resulting `lineplot.result$Plot` is a ggplot object, which can be
further modified by the user if desired.

```{r}
#Subset the example granges object down to only chrX
chrx.granges <- granges[GenomicRanges::seqnames(granges)=="chrX"]
lineplot.result <- SCCNVis::makeLinePlot(obj, gr = chrx.granges,
                                         clusters = clusters,
                                         show.x.ticks = TRUE,
                                         ylab="Copy Ratio",
                                         cluster.label = "Subclone")

#Save the plot. Not running this here
#SCCNVis::saveCustomPlot(lineplot.result$Plot, "lineplot.png")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example 1b. Lineplot of chrX", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("1b_lineplot.png")
```
